title: World Leaders Meet at the UN to Talk About War, AI, and a Warming Planet
summary:
What if you got all the most powerful leaders on Earth into one building? That's basically what's happening at the United Nations in New York this week. About 130 presidents and prime ministers are showing up to talk about the world's biggest problems.

What's on the list? Wars that won't stop, climate change making life harder for millions, prices going up, and a new fear: artificial intelligence (AI) — computer programs that can think and learn — growing so fast that no one has rules for it yet.

The United Nations is 81 years old. It was started by the winners of World War II. Now, some countries say it's time to update how it works, including the powerful Security Council, where five countries — the U.S., Russia, China, Britain, and France — can say "no" to any big decision.

U.S. President Donald Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron speak on Tuesday. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian speak Wednesday. But some leaders aren't coming. China's President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington instead. Russia's Vladimir Putin and India's Narendra Modi are skipping too.

The UN has had a tough year. The U.S. owed billions of dollars, but recently paid $725 million to keep its vote. One expert said the UN isn't in "emergency care" anymore, but it's "trapped in a trauma center."
why_it_matters: Decisions made in that big building can change the price of things your family buys, whether countries stay safe, and what rules will govern the new AI tools kids are already using.

keywords.explanation: A group where almost all the countries in the world meet to talk about big world problems.
A giant war fought between many countries around the world, long before your parents were born; the United Nations was started afterwards.
The part of the United Nations that makes the strongest decisions — five countries in it can say 'no' to any big decision.
Computer programs that can think, learn and do jobs that used to need a person.
Long-term changes in Earth's weather, such as the planet getting warmer, which makes life harder for many people.
A special part of a hospital where very seriously hurt people are treated — here it is used as a way to say the UN is badly shaken.

background_read: The United Nations (a group where almost all countries in the world meet to talk about big problems like wars and hunger) holds a huge meeting in New York every September, and leaders give speeches about what their countries want.

The Security Council (the part of the United Nations that makes the strongest decisions) has five members that never change — the U.S., Russia, China, Britain and France — and each one can block a decision by saying 'no'.

Countries are supposed to pay money to the United Nations to keep it running, and a country that falls far behind can lose its vote; that is why the U.S. payment mattered, since it had owed billions of dollars.
Article_Structure: WHO: About 130 presidents and prime ministers, including U.S. President Donald Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron, plus Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian — while China's Xi Jinping, Russia's Vladimir Putin and India's Narendra Modi skip it.
WHAT: The yearly meeting at the United Nations, where leaders talk about wars, climate change, rising prices and artificial intelligence that has no rules yet.
WHERE: The United Nations in New York, with a side meeting between Trump and Xi Jinping in Washington.
WHY: Some countries say the 81-year-old United Nations, started by the winners of World War II, needs updating — including the Security Council — and the UN has had a tough year with money problems.

perspectives.description: Some countries say the United Nations is 81 years old and needs to change how it works, especially the Security Council, so that more of the world gets a say in big decisions.
China's Xi Jinping, Russia's Vladimir Putin and India's Narendra Modi are skipping the meeting, which some see as a sign that they think the UN is not the place where real deals get done.
One expert said the UN is no longer in 'emergency care' but is still 'trapped in a trauma center' — meaning it is surviving, but it is still in a very shaky state.
